short: The Central Asian khanate that stayed nomadic longest and broke in two in 1347.
full:
Chagatai, Genghis Khan's second son, received the lands between the Altai and the Amu Darya — Transoxiana and the Tarim Basin — as his ulus. He was the family's authority on the yasa, the Mongol legal code, and had a reputation for enforcing it harshly. His successors held territory that included Samarkand and Bukhara but for decades governed it at arm's length, taxing the oasis cities through Muslim revenue farmers while the ruling house stayed on the grasslands.

That tension defined the khanate. Khans who settled and converted to Islam, such as Tarmashirin in the 1330s, were overthrown by the nomadic aristocracy; khans who stayed on the steppe lost their grip on the cities. In 1347 the state split for good, into Moghulistan in the east and a Transoxiana where Turco-Mongol amirs ruled through puppet khans. From that western half emerged Timur, who took power in 1370 and never claimed the title of khan himself, ruling instead as amir in the name of a Chagatayid figurehead.
